Family Health

A dilated pore of Winer is more than an ordinary visible pore

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A persistent opening with a dark plug can resemble a large blackhead, but it may be a specific follicular lesion. An examination helps establish what it is before you choose a treatment or try to remove it.

A specific follicular lesion, not simply visible pores

A dilated pore of Winer is a benign growth arising from the upper part of a hair follicle. The medical word tumour can sound alarming, but here it describes a noncancerous lesion. It is not a diagnosis for everyone who notices large pores across their nose or cheeks. It also should not be described as a sweat-gland problem without qualification.

Louis H. Winer described the condition in 1954, which is why his name appears in its title. The opening often contains a dark plug of keratin, a protein also found in skin, hair and nails. It can resemble an unusually large blackhead. Its deeper structure explains why taking out the visible material is different from removing the lesion itself.

What you may notice on the skin

The usual pattern is a single enlarged, roughly round opening with a dark centre and otherwise normal-looking skin around it. It often occurs on the face, head or neck, although the torso, particularly the back, can also be affected. A typical uncomplicated lesion does not hurt, and it may attract attention mainly because of its appearance.

These features are a description, not a way to confirm a diagnosis from a photograph. Pain, warmth, swelling or discharge can develop after repeated picking or squeezing, and a new or changing lump may have another cause. Tell a clinician how long it has been there, whether it has changed and whether you have tried to empty it.

The cause and risk factors are not a personal fault

The exact cause is uncertain. Proposed explanations have included changes around a follicular cyst and reactive thickening of its lining. A theory involving surrounding scar tissue should not be presented as a proven sequence that happens in every case. The condition is recognised as a distinct follicular lesion rather than simply the result of dirt trapped in skin.

Reports describe it more often in middle-aged or older adults, particularly men over forty, and more frequently in white populations. It can occur in other groups and occasionally younger adults, so those patterns cannot rule it in or out. A history of severe inflammatory or cystic acne has been associated with it. Having one does not show that you failed to follow a skincare routine.

Several other growths can look similar

An ordinary comedone, an epidermoid cyst, a pilar cyst and other follicular growths can have overlapping features. Less familiar names include a hair-follicle naevus and sebaceous trichofolliculoma, a benign follicular lesion. They are not all interchangeable types of blocked pore, and you do not need to identify them yourself before arranging an appointment.

Pilar sheath acanthoma is another benign growth that can be particularly difficult to distinguish. It often appears on the upper lip with a small central opening. Differences in symmetry or location may help the examination, but cannot settle the diagnosis alone. When necessary, a small tissue sample examined under a microscope can show the characteristic structure.

When examination or a biopsy is useful

A clinician can often recognise a typical dilated pore during an examination. A biopsy is not compulsory for every stable, uncomplicated lesion. It may be recommended if the appearance is unusual, the diagnosis is uncertain or the lesion is being removed. Ask whether the sample will be sent for pathology and how the result will reach you.

Rare reports have described a skin cancer such as basal cell carcinoma alongside or within a lesion described as a dilated pore. These reports do not mean an ordinary dilated pore is expected to become cancer. They reinforce the need to assess a growth that bleeds, ulcerates, changes rapidly or does not fit the usual pattern. Avoid squeezing it before the appointment, since inflammation can obscure the appearance.

Observation and temporary extraction are different choices

Once the diagnosis is secure, a painless lesion may be left alone. Wanting advice about its appearance is reasonable, but removal is not automatically necessary for health. There is no established cream or home remedy that reliably removes the entire structure. Acne treatment for the surrounding skin is a separate question.

A professional may empty the keratin plug with a comedone extractor, a small instrument with an opening that applies controlled pressure. The visible centre may improve, but the remaining lining can produce more material and refill. Repeated home extraction, forceful squeezing or digging with a needle can cause inflammation, infection and scarring. Temporary flattening should not be mistaken for a permanent cure.

Why surface treatments and complete removal differ

Freezing, dermabrasion, electrocautery and laser procedures have been used to alter these lesions. Their limitation is that the base can extend deeper than the treatment reaches. If the lining remains, the opening may refill or recur. Ask what a proposed treatment actually removes and what evidence supports it for this diagnosis, rather than assuming every cosmetic method has the same result.

Excision, sometimes with a punch technique, aims to remove the whole lesion and is usually curative when complete. This is often an office procedure using local anaesthetic. Size, depth, site and diagnostic uncertainty guide the choice. Incomplete removal can recur, and even successful removal may leave a scar. A published report or an individual successful case cannot guarantee an identical cosmetic outcome for you.

Discuss procedural risks and follow the wound plan

Bleeding, infection and scarring are possible after removal. Before treatment, mention medicines that affect bleeding, previous wound problems and a tendency to develop raised scars. Ask about stitches, dressings, expected healing and follow-up. The aim is to weigh the benefit of removing the opening against the appearance and care needs of the healing wound.

Follow the dermatologist’s instructions for gentle cleaning and dressings. Keeping a wound clean does not usually mean letting it dry out: skin-biopsy guidance often uses petroleum jelly and a covering to support moist healing. Avoid scrubbing, acids and unadvised antiseptics on the site. Increasing warmth, swelling, pain, spreading redness, pus or fever needs prompt advice, as does bleeding that does not stop with the instructed pressure.

There is no proven routine that prevents every lesion

Because the cause is not fully understood, no cleansing product can promise prevention. Appropriate acne care, gentle washing and sun protection support general skin health, but they do not guarantee that a dilated pore will never appear. Repeated exfoliation can irritate skin without changing the underlying follicular structure.

If a treated opening refills, arrange review rather than repeatedly removing the plug yourself. Bring any earlier diagnosis or pathology report to the appointment. For a stable confirmed lesion, observation may remain a comfortable choice; for uncertainty, symptoms or a cosmetic concern, a dermatologist can explain the available options and their limits.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Clinical descriptions distinguish a dilated pore of Winer from general pore visibility and identify it as a benign follicular growth.

A secure diagnosis may need no treatment; plug extraction can recur, while complete removal has procedural tradeoffs.

How BeMama can help

Before a skin appointment, note when the lesion appeared and any changes or previous treatment. Ask whether observation is reasonable and how a pathology result would be communicated.

When to seek help

Arrange assessment for a changing, bleeding, ulcerated or persistently painful lesion. After removal, increasing warmth, swelling, pus, fever or continuing bleeding needs prompt medical advice.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A dilated pore is a specific follicular lesion.
  • Its appearance can overlap with other skin growths.
  • An uncomplicated confirmed lesion can often be observed.
  • Extraction may leave a lining that refills.
  • Complete removal can leave a scar and needs aftercare.

Frequently asked questions

Do generally large facial pores mean I have this condition?

No. A dilated pore of Winer usually describes a particular persistent lesion, often solitary, rather than all the visible pores on the face.

Does the word tumour mean cancer?

Not in this diagnosis. It describes a benign follicular growth. A clinician should still assess an uncertain or changing lesion rather than applying the label from appearance alone.

Is the dark centre caused by poor hygiene?

A dark keratin plug is not proof of poor hygiene. The cause of the lesion is not fully established, and aggressive washing does not remove its deeper structure.

Can people under forty have one?

Yes. It is reported more often in older adults, but age and demographic patterns do not establish or exclude the diagnosis.

Does everyone need a biopsy?

No. A typical lesion may be diagnosed clinically. A biopsy can help when the diagnosis is uncertain or when tissue is removed.

What is pilar sheath acanthoma?

It is another benign follicular growth, often near the upper lip, that can resemble a dilated pore. Tissue examination may be needed to distinguish them.

Will squeezing out the plug cure it?

Not necessarily. The lining may remain and refill with keratin. Home squeezing also risks inflammation, infection and scarring.

Are laser or freezing treatments always permanent?

No. They may not reach the deeper lining. Ask why a particular technique is being recommended and what recurrence or scarring to expect.

Is surgical removal guaranteed to leave no mark?

No. Complete removal is usually effective, but a scar and other procedural risks remain. Discuss the likely appearance before choosing it.

Should I dry out the wound after removal?

Follow the clinic’s wound plan. Dermatology guidance commonly supports gentle cleaning and moist, covered healing, rather than scrubbing or deliberately drying the wound.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
